title: Political transformations and their effects on foods in Peru, Venezuela and Argentina
abstract:
Eating is an indispensable part of the life of any animal, it takes up a great part of our time. However, for thousands of years, humans have been doing it differently, being food one of the clearest examples of how we have converted nature into culture. Eating is still a biological necessity that defines us merely as living beings, but the way we eat and cook can say a lot about how we organize our societies and how we relate with one another and our environments. Some have come as far as to say that what makes us different from animals are precisely our gastronomies.
This is why we believe that, by getting to know how foods and everything that surrounds them change, we can better understand ourselves and what matters to us. We think that, by understanding how politics can affect something as close to our daily lives as food, we can get a new perspective on the multiple effects that political changes have on people.
In this research which examines the ways in which political transformations have an impact on the gastronomies of Argentina, Venezuela and Peru, we analyzed during three months academic papers as well as articles from local magazines and newspapers that talked indirectly about foods. We then identified some of the topics that we saw repeatedly and developed an interview seeking to understand how these different topics related to each other and gave a meaning to foods. Finally, we compared and contrasted the results from our interview with other ideas that we had previously seen in our analyses.
As a conclusion, we found out that food in these countries plays a very important role in the development of a collective identity at multiple levels: familiar, local and national. Because of the social nature of food in these societies, it is especially vulnerable to political phenomena and two of the greatest ones so far have been migration and globalization. Both of them have had multiple consequences on foods like their loss of relevance within the family unit.
